meta.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
meta.status: SAMPLE / UNVERIFIED study aid. Constitutional articles and figures can change through amendment; verify against the current text of the Constitution.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: What is the separation of powers and how is it reflected in Pakistan's Constitution?
questions.expected_answer: Separation of powers divides state authority among the legislature, the executive and the judiciary so that each acts as a check on the others. In Pakistan's 1973 Constitution the legislature is Parliament (the National Assembly and the Senate), the executive is the President, the Prime Minister and the Cabinet in a parliamentary system, and the judiciary is headed by the Supreme Court. In practice the boundaries and balance have been contested over time.
evaluation_criteria: Defines separation of powers and checks and balances
Maps the three organs to Pakistan's institutions
questions.explanation: A foundational concept; strong answers go beyond definition to institutional mapping.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: Describe the main features of the Eighteenth Amendment to the Constitution of Pakistan.
questions.expected_answer: Passed in April 2010, it removed the President's power to dissolve the National Assembly, abolished the Concurrent Legislative List and devolved subjects to the provinces, renamed the North-West Frontier Province as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, strengthened the Council of Common Interests, and inserted rights such as the right to education (Article 25A) and the right to information (Article 19A). It also changed the procedure for judicial appointments through a Judicial Commission and a parliamentary committee.
evaluation_criteria: Gives the year and main purpose
Lists at least four specific changes
questions.explanation: An important constitutional change; list specific provisions and the federal impact.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: Evaluate the challenges of local government in Pakistan and its constitutional position.
questions.expected_answer: Article 140A, inserted by the Eighteenth Amendment, requires each province to establish a local government system and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility to elected local bodies. In practice, local government has been strongest under military governments (Basic Democracies, the 2001 devolution plan), which raised questions of legitimacy, while elected governments have been reluctant to devolve. Challenges include irregular local elections, limited fiscal autonomy, overlap with provincial departments and weak capacity.
questions.explanation: Evaluation requires both constitutional obligations and the gap in practice.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: What are Fundamental Rights under the 1973 Constitution? Name and explain at least five.
questions.expected_answer: Fundamental Rights are in Part II, Chapter 1 of the Constitution (Articles 8-28), and laws inconsistent with them are void (Article 8). They include security of person (Article 9), safeguards on arrest and detention (Article 10), the right to a fair trial (Article 10A), inviolability of dignity (Article 14), freedom of movement (Article 15), freedom of association (Article 17), freedom of speech (Article 19), the right to information (Article 19A), freedom of religion (Article 20), the right to property (Article 23), equality of citizens (Article 25) and the right to education (Article 25A).
evaluation_criteria: Locates fundamental rights in the Constitution
Names at least five with article numbers
Notes that laws inconsistent with them are void
questions.explanation: Recall plus accurate article numbers; the Article 8 principle shows deeper understanding.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: What is the role of the civil service in governance, and how is the federal civil service recruited and organised?
questions.expected_answer: The civil service implements government policy, delivers public services and provides continuity and technical expertise across changes of government. At the federal level recruitment is mainly through the Federal Public Service Commission (established under the Constitution, Article 242) via the Central Superior Services competitive examination; officers serve in occupational groups and are placed in basic pay scales (BPS 1 to 22). Principles include merit, neutrality and accountability.
evaluation_criteria: Explains the role of the civil service
Describes recruitment through FPSC and CSS
Mentions principles such as merit and neutrality
questions.explanation: Directly relevant to the examination: show awareness of the institution's role and recruitment.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: How does the Senate differ from the National Assembly in Pakistan's Parliament?
questions.expected_answer: The National Assembly is the lower house, directly elected on the basis of population, and the Prime Minister must command its confidence; money bills originate there. The Senate is the upper house in which the federating units have equal representation, giving smaller provinces a voice in federal legislation. Senators are elected indirectly for six-year terms, and the Senate is a permanent house that is not dissolved, with half of its members retiring every three years.
evaluation_criteria: Explains the representation basis of each house
Mentions the term and permanence of the Senate
questions.explanation: Compare along representation, election method, term and powers.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: Describe the structure of the judicial system of Pakistan and the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
questions.expected_answer: The superior judiciary consists of the Supreme Court, the Federal Shariat Court and the High Courts (including the Islamabad High Court); below them are district and sessions courts and other subordinate and special courts. The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction in disputes between governments (Article 184(1)) and in matters of public importance involving fundamental rights (Article 184(3)), while High Courts issue writs for enforcement of rights under Article 199.
questions.explanation: Hierarchy plus article references is the pattern for judicial-structure answers.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: Explain the National Finance Commission (NFC) Award and the debates around the distribution of resources between the federation and the provinces.
questions.expected_answer: Under Article 160, the NFC is constituted periodically to recommend how the divisible pool of federal taxes is distributed between the federation and the provinces and among the provinces. The 7th NFC Award (2010) moved from a population-only formula to multiple criteria (population, poverty, revenue generation and inverse population density) and raised the provinces' share of the divisible pool to 57.5 percent. Debates concern the federal government's reduced fiscal space, provincial capacity to spend and raise revenue, and whether the formula should change.
evaluation_criteria: Explains the NFC and divisible pool
questions.explanation: Fiscal federalism: explain the mechanism and the tension between federal and provincial needs.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: Describe the procedure for amending the Constitution of Pakistan and explain the debate about limits on Parliament's amending power.
questions.expected_answer: Under Article 239, a constitutional amendment bill must be passed by at least a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each house; amendments affecting the limits of a province also need that province's assembly approval and the President's assent. The debate concerns whether Parliament can alter the Constitution's salient features such as federalism, parliamentary democracy and judicial independence; courts have considered the question in cases like the 2015 judgment on the 18th and 21st Amendments, with differing opinions.
evaluation_criteria: Explains the basic structure/salient features debate
Refers to judicial treatment of the issue
questions.explanation: Procedure plus a conceptual debate; keep the court position described with care.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: What are judicial review and suo motu jurisdiction? Discuss their strengths and criticisms.
questions.expected_answer: Judicial review is the power of courts to examine whether legislation or executive action conforms to the Constitution and to strike down what does not. Suo motu jurisdiction allows the Supreme Court to take notice of matters of public importance involving fundamental rights on its own motion under Article 184(3). Supporters say these powers protect rights and check abuses; critics argue that overuse leads to judicial overreach, undermines separation of powers and creates inconsistency. Parliament enacted the Supreme Court (Practice and Procedure) Act 2023 to regulate the use of suo motu powers.
questions.explanation: Balanced evaluation question; avoid taking sides without reasons.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: What is good governance? Explain its key principles.
questions.expected_answer: Good governance is the process of making and implementing decisions in a way that is accountable, transparent and responsive to citizens. Commonly cited principles are participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, consensus orientation, equity and inclusiveness, effectiveness and efficiency, and accountability. It is associated with better public services, reduced corruption and sustainable development.
questions.explanation: Stronger answers apply each principle to Pakistan with a brief example.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: Explain the Council of Common Interests and its role in Pakistan's federal system.
questions.expected_answer: The Council of Common Interests (Articles 153-154) is a constitutional body chaired by the Prime Minister with the provincial Chief Ministers and federal members as its members. It formulates and regulates policies in relation to matters in Part II of the Federal Legislative List and oversees related institutions, and it settles inter-provincial and federal-provincial disputes on subjects such as water and power. The Eighteenth Amendment strengthened it by requiring it to meet at least once every ninety days.
evaluation_criteria: Shows the effect of the Eighteenth Amendment
questions.explanation: Shows understanding of the institutional mechanism for cooperative federalism.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: Evaluate the accountability institutions in Pakistan such as the National Accountability Bureau, the Auditor-General and the Ombudsman.
questions.expected_answer: The Auditor-General of Pakistan (Articles 168-171) audits federal and provincial accounts and reports to the legislature, supporting parliamentary oversight. The Wafaqi Mohtasib (Federal Ombudsman, established 1983) investigates complaints of maladministration by federal agencies. The National Accountability Bureau, created by the 1999 ordinance, investigates and prosecutes corruption. Strengths include a legal mandate and public access; weaknesses include allegations of political bias, weak follow-up on audit findings, overlapping institutions and limited prosecutorial success. Reforms focus on independence, transparency and parliamentary follow-up.
evaluation_criteria: Describes the role of each institution accurately
questions.explanation: An evaluation across several bodies: structure by function, then assess effectiveness.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: Discuss the constitutional protection of religious minorities in Pakistan and the challenges in implementing it.
questions.expected_answer: The Constitution guarantees freedom of religion (Article 20), safeguards against discrimination (Articles 22 and 27), equality of citizens (Article 25), and directs the state to protect the legitimate rights and interests of minorities (Article 36); seats are reserved for non-Muslims in the legislatures. Challenges include discriminatory practices, misuse of blasphemy accusations, forced conversion complaints, discrimination in education and employment, and inadequate enforcement. In 2014 the Supreme Court directed the government to establish a task force and measures to protect minority rights. Solutions include education reform, legal safeguards against misuse, and stronger enforcement.
questions.explanation: A rights-based question: contrast legal guarantees with the practical situation.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: How can e-governance and digital public services improve service delivery in Pakistan, and what obstacles exist?
questions.expected_answer: E-governance can reduce corruption and delays through online services, digital identity and payments, open data and transparent records. Examples include national identity registration and online tax filing and complaint systems. Obstacles include limited internet access and digital literacy, fragmented systems and weak data protection, resistance from officials who benefit from discretion, inadequate funding and cybersecurity risks. Success depends on leadership, interoperable systems, citizen-centred design and legal safeguards.
questions.explanation: Policy question: tie each obstacle to a corresponding reform.

questions.subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
questions.question: Analyse the relationship between the executive and Parliament in a parliamentary system, with reference to Pakistan.
questions.expected_answer: In a parliamentary system the executive is drawn from and accountable to the legislature. In Pakistan the Prime Minister, who must command the confidence of the National Assembly, is the chief executive (Article 90), the Cabinet is collectively responsible to Parliament (Article 91), and the President acts on the advice of the Prime Minister (Article 48). Parliament can remove the government through a vote of no confidence (Article 95) and oversees it through committees, questions and budgets. Weaknesses in practice include weak committee systems, dominance of the executive, and the effect of defection rules (Article 63A) on legislators' independence.
evaluation_criteria: Explains accountability of the executive to Parliament
questions.explanation: Combine constitutional theory with an honest view of how oversight works in practice.
